name: Jana Novotná
milestone_by_age_26: Won her first WTA Tour singles title at Adelaide in 1988 (age 19) and reached the 1991 Australian Open singles final (age 22).
early_history_summary: Born in Brno, Czechoslovakia, Novotná started playing tennis at age 8 and joined a tennis club at 14. She turned professional in February 1987 at age 18, relatively late by modern standards, and quickly established herself as a top doubles player before breaking through in singles in the late 1980s.
family_context_summary: Father was an engineer and mother was a teacher in Brno; both were keen on sport but there was no particular emphasis on tennis. She grew up during the communist era in Czechoslovakia.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Czechoslovak tennis system, national team pipeline, coach Hana Mandlikova
evidence_summary: Novotná grew up in Brno with an engineer father and teacher mother, both sport-oriented but without tennis-specific backgrounds. She advanced through Czechoslovak junior tennis programs and turned pro at 18, benefiting from the national sports system that produced many tennis champions. Her early career was primarily in doubles before transitioning to singles success. The communist-era sports infrastructure provided structured training and competitive opportunities, though facilities were limited compared to Western standards.
starting_point: Born to an engineer father and teacher mother in Brno, Czechoslovakia; both parents were sport-oriented but had no particular tennis background.
current_position: Died on 19 November 2017 at age 49 from ovarian cancer in the Czech Republic; final role: retired tennis champion and coach to Barbora Krejcikova.

trajectory.event: Won her first WTA Tour singles title at Adelaide and Olympic silver medal in doubles at Seoul.
Reached the Australian Open singles final, losing to Monica Seles.
Reached the Wimbledon singles final against Steffi Graf, famously crying on the Duchess of Kent's shoulder after surrendering a lead.
Won the Wimbledon singles championship, her first and only Grand Slam singles title, defeating Nathalie Tauziat.
Retired from professional tennis with 24 singles titles and 76 doubles titles.
Inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame.
Died of ovarian cancer on 19 November 2017 in the Czech Republic.

name: Mika Salo
milestone_by_age_26: Won the European Formula Ford 1600 Championship in 1988 with 14 wins from 14 races, and finished 2nd in the British Formula 3 Championship in 1990 with 6 wins.
early_history_summary: Born in Helsinki, Salo began karting at age 5 after his racing-enthusiast father took him to the Keimola circuit. He won his first race at age 6 and was Finnish Go-Kart Champion by 1978 (age 12). He progressed through Formula Ford and British Formula 3 before racing in Japanese F3000, eventually reaching Formula One in 1994 at age 27.
family_context_summary: Father liked racing and took young Mika to the Keimola circuit; father's company had a corporate karting day where Mika first got behind the wheel. No documented financial or professional racing background in the family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a racing enthusiast who introduced Mika to karting at age 5, providing early exposure to the sport but no documented professional racing expertise.
primary_early_advantage_tags: karting from age 5, father racing enthusiasm, Finnish karting pipeline
evidence_summary: Salo's father, a racing enthusiast, introduced him to karting at age 5 at the Keimola circuit near Helsinki. He started racing at 6 and won the Finnish Go-Kart Championship at 12, building exceptional early reps in motorsport. He progressed through Formula Ford (winning the European championship in 1988) and British F3 (finishing 2nd to Mika Häkkinen in 1990) before spending four years in Japanese F3000. His F1 debut came at 27, relatively late, suggesting his junior career was strong but not enough to fast-track him to the top.
starting_point: Born in Helsinki, Finland; father was a racing enthusiast who introduced him to karting at age 5 through a corporate karting event at the Keimola circuit.
current_position: Retired from racing; works as a Formula One broadcaster and commentator; resides in London, England.

trajectory.event: Won the Finnish Go-Kart Championship, establishing himself as a promising young karter.
Won the European Formula Ford 1600 Championship with 14 wins from 14 races, dominating the series.
Finished 2nd in the British Formula 3 Championship with 6 wins, losing the title to Mika Häkkinen.
Made Formula One debut with Lotus at the Japanese Grand Prix.
Stood in for injured Michael Schumacher at Ferrari, scoring two podiums including 2nd at the German Grand Prix.
Raced for Toyota in their Formula One debut season, his final year in F1.
Won the 24 Hours of Le Mans in the GT2 class for the second consecutive year.

name: Kenny Dalglish
milestone_by_age_26: Became a Celtic first-team regular and made his Scotland national team debut in 1971 (age 20), going on to win four Scottish league championships before signing for Liverpool in 1977 for a British record fee.
early_history_summary: Born in Dalmarnock, Glasgow, the son of an engineer, Dalglish grew up supporting Rangers but signed for Celtic in 1967. He was farmed out to Cumbernauld United and worked as an apprentice joiner before breaking into Celtic's first team in 1971 at age 20, becoming a key player in their dominant era.
family_context_summary: Son of an engineer from Dalmarnock in Glasgow's east end; grew up in Milton in the north of the city and moved to a tower block in Ibrox at age 14. Working-class Glasgow upbringing.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources; no evidence of football connections in the family despite growing up in Glasgow's football culture.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Glasgow football culture, Celtic youth system, Quality Street Gang reserves, Jock Stein mentorship
evidence_summary: Dalglish grew up in a working-class Glasgow family, the son of an engineer, immersed in one of the world's most intense football cultures. He won the Scottish Cup with Glasgow Schoolboys and was selected for Scottish schoolboys before signing for Celtic in 1967. Celtic's legendary manager Jock Stein and assistant Sean Fallon personally recruited him. He developed in Celtic's renowned reserve team (the 'Quality Street Gang') before breaking into the first team at 20, benefiting from the club's European Cup-winning infrastructure and the broader Scottish football pipeline that produced many world-class players.
starting_point: Born to an engineer father in Dalmarnock, Glasgow's east end; working-class upbringing in Milton and later Ibrox, immersed in Glasgow's intense football culture.
current_position: Retired Scottish football legend; knighthood (Sir Kenny); widely regarded as one of the greatest British footballers of all time; estimated net worth in the millions; resides in Scotland.

trajectory.event: Made Celtic first-team debut as a substitute in a League Cup match against Hamilton Academical.
Established himself as a Celtic first-team regular and made his Scotland national team debut against Belgium.
Won the Scottish league championship with Celtic, the first of four league titles with the club.
Signed for Liverpool for a British record fee of £440,000, replacing Kevin Keegan.
Scored the winning goal in the European Cup final against FC Bruges, clinching Liverpool's second consecutive European Cup.
Won the Ballon d'Or Silver Award and PFA Players' Player of the Year after Liverpool's treble-winning season.
Became Liverpool player-manager following Joe Fagan's resignation, winning the league and FA Cup in his first season.
Named the greatest striker in post-war British football by FourFourTwo magazine.

name: Elle Macpherson
milestone_by_age_26: Appeared on the cover of the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue for three consecutive years (1986-1988) and was nicknamed 'The Body' by Time magazine in 1989, establishing herself as one of the world's top models by age 25.
early_history_summary: Born Eleanor Nancy Gow in Killara, Sydney, Macpherson grew up on Sydney's North Shore and planned to study law at the University of Sydney. Before starting university, she traveled to the US in 1982 at age 18 for modeling work to pay for law books, signing with Click Model Management in New York and quickly rising to prominence through commercials and magazine covers.
family_context_summary: Daughter of entrepreneur and sound engineer Peter Gow (former president of the Cronulla-Sutherland Sharks rugby league team) and nurse Frances Gow. Parents divorced when she was 10; she moved with her mother and siblings, and her surname changed to Macpherson (her stepfather's name) due to a clerical error at school.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an entrepreneur and sound engineer who served as president of a Sydney rugby league team, providing a background in business and public-facing roles, though not directly in modeling or fashion.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Sports Illustrated platform, Click Model Management, physical attributes, 1980s supermodel wave
evidence_summary: Macpherson grew up in a middle-class Sydney family; her father was an entrepreneur and rugby league club president, her mother a nurse. After her parents' divorce, she was raised by her mother and stepfather on Sydney's North Shore. She was discovered at 18 while on vacation in Aspen, Colorado, and signed with Click Model Management in New York. Her striking physical attributes (6 feet tall) and the 1980s supermodel cultural wave propelled her to rapid fame, with three consecutive SI Swimsuit covers from 1986-1988 cementing her status as a global icon by her mid-twenties.
starting_point: Born to entrepreneur/sound engineer Peter Gow and nurse Frances Gow in Killara, Sydney; middle-class upbringing on Sydney's North Shore; parents divorced when she was 10.
current_position: Australian supermodel and businesswoman; founder of Elle Macpherson Intimates lingerie line and The Body skincare; estimated net worth approximately $95 million; resides between London, New York, and Sydney.

trajectory.event: Signed with Click Model Management in New York and landed her first TV commercial for Tab cola.
Appeared on her first Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue cover, beginning a record-setting run of five covers.
Nicknamed 'The Body' by Time magazine, cementing her status as a global supermodel.
Acted in the film Sirens alongside Hugh Grant and posed for Playboy magazine.
Launched the Elle Macpherson 'The Body' skincare range, expanding her business empire.
Became host and executive producer of Britain & Ireland's Next Top Model, transitioning to television.

name: Herzi Halevi
milestone_by_age_26: No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 found. Halevi began military service in 1985 and was a young officer in the paratroopers and Sayeret Matkal, but his major commands (Sayeret Matkal commander in 2001, IDF Chief of Staff in 2023) came well after age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Jerusalem to a religious family with deep roots in Israeli history, Halevi began his IDF service in 1985 at age 17, joining the paratrooper brigade. He completed officer training and moved to the elite Sayeret Matkal reconnaissance unit, but his significant command roles came decades later.
family_context_summary: Born in Jerusalem to a religious Jewish family; father is a descendant of Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook, the first chief rabbi of Israel. Named after his uncle, a paratrooper killed in the Six-Day War in 1967.
parent_family_domain_summary: Family has deep religious and military heritage; father descended from a prominent rabbinical lineage, and an uncle was killed in combat as a paratrooper, creating a strong military-service family tradition.
evidence_summary: Halevi was born into a prominent religious Jerusalem family with deep connections to Israel's founding history. He began military service at 17 in 1985, joining the paratroopers before moving to the elite Sayeret Matkal unit. While his military career was underway by his early twenties, no specific material milestone (major command, decoration, or public recognition) has been documented by age 26. His significant achievements — commanding Sayeret Matkal (2001), heading Military Intelligence, and becoming IDF Chief of Staff (2023) — all came well after age 26.

name: Guido Crepax
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Palme d'Or for advertising in 1957 for his Shell Oil publicity campaign, and graduated in architecture from Milan University (Politecnico) in 1958, establishing himself as a successful graphic artist by his mid-twenties.
early_history_summary: Born in Milan to a prominent musical family — his father Gilberto was a cellist at La Scala and professor at the Milanese Conservatory — Crepax drew comics from his early teens. He studied architecture at the Politecnico di Milano, graduating in 1958, while already working as a commercial graphic artist designing advertising posters, record sleeves, and book covers.
family_context_summary: Born into a cultured Milanese family; father Gilberto Crepax was a prominent cellist who played at Teatro alla Scala under Arturo Toscanini and became a professor at the Milanese Conservatory. Brother Franco became a music producer and director of GGD-CBS record company.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a prominent professional musician (cellist at La Scala and conservatory professor), and brother was a music industry executive, providing a rich cultural and artistic upbringing that influenced Crepax's aesthetic sensibility, though not directly in comics or graphic design.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Milan cultural milieu, musician father, Politecnico architecture training, early drawing
evidence_summary: Crepax grew up in a culturally rich Milanese household; his father was a prominent cellist at La Scala and his brother a music industry executive, immersing him in art and aesthetics from childhood. He drew comics from his early teens and studied architecture at the Politecnico di Milano, graduating in 1958. By his mid-twenties he was already an accomplished commercial graphic artist, winning the Palme d'Or for advertising in 1957 for his Shell Oil campaign. His architectural training and musical family background deeply informed the sophisticated visual style that later made his comic Valentina (1965) an iconic work of European comics.
starting_point: Born in Milan, Italy to a prominent musical family; father Gilberto was a cellist at Teatro alla Scala who became first cellist under Arturo Toscanini and a professor at the Milanese Conservatory.
current_position: Died on 31 July 2003 at age 70 in Milan, Italy; final role: celebrated Italian comic artist best known for the Valentina series (1965-1995).

trajectory.event: Won the Palme d'Or for advertising for his Shell Oil publicity campaign, establishing himself as a leading graphic designer.
Graduated in architecture from the Politecnico di Milano while already working as a commercial illustrator.
Created the character Valentina, published in Linus magazine, which became his signature work and an icon of 1960s Italian culture.
Won the Yellow Kid Award and the Adamson Award for his contributions to international comics.
A film adaptation of his work, Baba Yaga featuring the character Valentina, was released.
Inducted into the Jack Kirby Hall of Fame for his contributions to comics.
Died on 31 July 2003 in Milan, Italy.

name: Luc Luycx
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Luycx was working as a computer engineer at the Royal Belgian Mint in his twenties; his major achievement, designing the common side of the euro coins, came in 1996-1997 at age 38-39.
early_history_summary: Born in Aalst, Belgium, Luycx worked as a computer engineer at the Royal Belgian Mint. He was introduced to coin design when his supervisor asked him to take a coin engraving course, learning CorelDRAW and transitioning to coin design. His euro coin design won a European competition in 1997.
evidence_summary: Luycx was born in Aalst, Belgium, and worked as a computer engineer at the Royal Belgian Mint. He was introduced to coin design relatively late when his supervisor asked him to take a coin engraving course, after which he learned CorelDRAW and developed a passion for designing coins. His major achievement — winning the European competition to design the common side of the euro coins — occurred in 1996-1997 when he was 38-39 years old, well beyond age 26. No material milestone by age 26 has been documented.

name: Elvira Saadi
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic team gold at the 1972 Munich Olympics (age 20) and a second Olympic team gold at the 1976 Montreal Olympics (age 24), plus World Championship team gold and floor exercise bronze in 1974.
early_history_summary: Born in Tashkent, Uzbek SSR, Saadi began gymnastics at the relatively late age of 12 in 1964 when her mother enrolled her in a junior gymnastic school. She joined the USSR national team in 1969 at age 17 and rose to become an Olympic champion by 20, known for her sensual, theatrical floor exercise routines.
family_context_summary: Born in Tashkent, Uzbek SSR; mother enrolled her in a junior gymnastic school at age 12. No documented information about father's profession or family financial status.
parent_family_domain_summary: Mother actively enrolled Elvira in gymnastics at age 12, showing parental initiative in sports training, but no documented professional gymnastics or athletic background in the family.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Soviet gymnastics system, Dynamo Tashkent/Moscow, coach Vladimir Aksyonov, USSR national team
evidence_summary: Saadi was born in Tashkent and entered gymnastics at 12 when her mother enrolled her in a junior gymnastic school. She joined the USSR national team at 17, benefiting from the Soviet Union's world-dominant gymnastics pipeline that provided elite coaching, facilities, and competitive opportunities. Her coach Vladimir Aksyonov moved with her to Moscow's Dynamo club in 1974 to train at the highest level. The Soviet sports system was a powerful accelerator, concentrating resources on promising athletes and providing the infrastructure that produced multiple Olympic champions. Saadi's distinctive artistic style on floor exercise set her apart among the celebrated Soviet gymnasts of the era.
starting_point: Born in Tashkent, Uzbek SSR (Soviet Union); mother enrolled her in a junior gymnastic school at age 12; no documented information about father's profession or family financial status.
current_position: Retired gymnast living in Canada; works as an elite gymnastics coach at Cambridge Kips club in Ontario, producing Canadian Olympians; inducted into International Gymnastics Hall of Fame in 2009.

trajectory.event: Joined the USSR national gymnastics team after training at Dynamo Tashkent.
Won Olympic team gold medal at the Munich Olympics and finished 8th in the all-around.
Won World Championship team gold and floor exercise bronze in Varna, having moved to Dynamo Moscow with coach Vladimir Aksyonov.
Won her second Olympic team gold medal at the Montreal Olympics.
Relocated to Canada to take a coaching position, beginning a new career as an elite gymnastics coach.
Inducted into the International Gymnastics Hall of Fame.

name: Nicola Cabibbo
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. Cabibbo graduated from Sapienza University of Rome in 1958 and was hired at the Frascati National Laboratories in 1960 as its first theoretical physicist, but his landmark achievement — the Cabibbo angle — was published in 1963 at age 28.
early_history_summary: Born in Rome to Sicilian parents, Cabibbo was interested in science from a young age, building his own radios. He studied physics at Sapienza University of Rome, graduating in 1958 with a thesis on weak interactions under Bruno Touschek, then worked at the INFN and Frascati laboratories before making his major discovery at CERN in 1963.
family_context_summary: Born in Rome to Sicilian parents; father Emanuele was a lawyer, mother was a housewife. Grew up during World War II but elementary education ran uninterrupted.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a lawyer, providing a middle-class professional household, but no documented scientific or academic background in the family. A textbook titled 'What Is Mathematics?' at the Liceo Torquato Tasso sparked his interest in science.
evidence_summary: Cabibbo was born in Rome to a lawyer father and housewife mother, both of Sicilian origin. He showed early interest in science, building radios as a youth, and was inspired by a mathematics textbook at his liceo. He enrolled at Sapienza University of Rome in 1952 and graduated in 1958 with a thesis on weak interactions under Bruno Touschek. He then worked at the INFN and Frascati laboratories. While he was a promising young physicist by 26, his landmark contribution — the Cabibbo angle, which explained weak decays of strange particles and paved the way for electroweak unification — was published in 1963 at age 28, just beyond the age-26 cutoff.

name: Mervyn Rose
milestone_by_age_26: Won the US Nationals doubles title in 1952 (age 22), repeated in 1953, and won the 1954 Australian Championships singles and doubles titles (age 24), representing Australia in Davis Cup from 1951.
early_history_summary: Born in Coffs Harbour, New South Wales, Rose was an aggressive left-hander who began playing on the amateur tennis tour from 1949 at age 19. He represented Australia in the Davis Cup from 1951 and won his first Grand Slam title at the 1952 US Nationals doubles, rising to become one of the world's top players by his mid-twenties.
family_context_summary: Born in Coffs Harbour, a coastal town in New South Wales, Australia. No documented information about parents' professions or family financial status in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Australian tennis system, Davis Cup team, Grand Slam circuit access, doubles partnerships
evidence_summary: Rose was born in the small coastal town of Coffs Harbour, NSW, with no documented family tennis background. He began competing on the amateur tennis tour at 19 in 1949, benefiting from Australia's dominant tennis infrastructure that produced a generation of world-class players in the 1950s. He represented Australia in the Davis Cup from 1951, giving him access to elite competition and team infrastructure. His aggressive left-handed playing style and strong volleying earned him Grand Slam doubles titles by 22 and a singles title at the 1954 Australian Championships at 24. The Australian tennis pipeline of the era was a powerful accelerator for talented players regardless of background.
starting_point: Born in Coffs Harbour, a small coastal town in New South Wales, Australia; no documented information about family profession or financial status.
current_position: Died on 23 July 2017 at age 87 in Coffs Harbour, New South Wales, Australia; final role: retired tennis champion and coach to players including Billie Jean King and Margaret Court.

trajectory.event: Began competing on the amateur tennis tour, reaching the third round of the Australian Championships.
Represented Australia in the Davis Cup for the first time, playing in the victorious final against the United States.
Won the US Nationals doubles title, his first Grand Slam championship.
Won the Australian Championships singles and doubles titles, defeating Ken Rosewall in the singles semifinal.
Won the French Championships singles title and was ranked World No. 3 by Lance Tingay of The Daily Telegraph.
Turned professional, joining Jack Kramer's group of contract players.
Inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame.
Died on 23 July 2017 in his hometown of Coffs Harbour, New South Wales.

name: Suzanne Morrow Francis
milestone_by_age_26: Won Olympic bronze medal in pairs at the 1948 Winter Olympics (age 17) with partner Wallace Diestelmeyer, also winning World Championship bronze and pioneering the one-handed death spiral; later won three consecutive Canadian singles titles (1949-1951).
early_history_summary: Born in Toronto, Ontario, Morrow Francis trained at the Toronto Skating Club and competed in both pairs and ladies' singles. With partner Wallace Diestelmeyer, she won the 1947 North American pairs title and 1948 Olympic bronze at age 17, before becoming Canadian singles champion from 1949 to 1951 and reaching 4th at the World Championships three times.
family_context_summary: Born in Toronto, Ontario, Canada. No documented information about parents' professions or family financial status in reviewed sources. She trained at the Toronto Skating Club.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Toronto Skating Club, pairs partnership with Diestelmeyer, Canadian figure skating system, Olympic exposure
evidence_summary: Morrow Francis was born in Toronto and trained at the Toronto Skating Club, one of Canada's premier figure skating institutions. She competed internationally by her mid-teens, winning the North American pairs title at 16 and Olympic bronze at 17 with partner Wallace Diestelmeyer. Their partnership was notable for innovating the one-handed death spiral, a technical first at the Olympic level. She also excelled in singles, winning three consecutive Canadian titles (1949-51) and reaching 4th at the World Championships. Her access to the Toronto Skating Club and competitive opportunities in the post-war Canadian figure skating system were key enablers, though family background details are not documented.
starting_point: Born in Toronto, Ontario, Canada; trained at the Toronto Skating Club; no documented information about family profession or financial status.
current_position: Died on 11 June 2006 at age 75 in Brantford, Ontario, Canada; final roles: retired veterinarian (practiced until 1995) and figure skating judge for over 50 years.

trajectory.event: Won the North American Senior pairs championship with partner Wallace Diestelmeyer and the Canadian pairs title.
Won Olympic bronze in pairs at the St. Moritz Winter Olympics and World Championship bronze, pioneering the one-handed death spiral in international competition.
Won the first of three consecutive Canadian women's singles championships.
Competed in her second Olympics in Oslo (6th in ladies' singles) and obtained a degree in veterinary medicine.
Became the first woman to take the Olympic judge's oath at the Calgary Winter Olympics.
Inducted into the Skate Canada Hall of Fame together with Wallace Diestelmeyer.
Died on 11 June 2006 in Brantford, Ontario, Canada.

name: Gianluca Vialli
milestone_by_age_26: Won the European Cup Winners' Cup with Sampdoria in 1990 (age 25), scoring both goals in the final, and had already won multiple Coppa Italia titles and become an established Italy international by age 26.
early_history_summary: Born in Cremona to a self-made millionaire father who owned a construction company, Vialli grew up in the Castello di Belgioso. He joined local club Pizzighettone at age 9, moved to Cremonese's youth system, and made his senior debut at 16 in Serie C1. His performances earned a transfer to Sampdoria in 1984 at age 20, where he formed the famous 'Goal Twins' partnership with Roberto Mancini.
family_context_summary: Born to a self-made millionaire father who owned a construction company; raised in the Castello di Belgioso in Cremona. Youngest of five children. The family was financially comfortable, but his father instilled a strong work ethic and ensured the children did not take life for granted.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a self-made millionaire construction company owner, providing significant financial security and a business-owner mindset, though not directly connected to football. The family's wealth allowed Vialli to grow up in a castle, but his father ensured he was not spoiled.
primary_early_advantage_tags: wealthy family, castle upbringing, Cremona football pipeline, Mancini partnership, Italian football system
evidence_summary: Vialli was born into unusual wealth for a footballer — his father was a self-made millionaire construction company owner, and the family lived in the Castello di Belgioso in Cremona. Despite this privilege, his father instilled a strong work ethic. Vialli showed football talent from age 9, joining Pizzighettone and then Cremonese, where he made his senior debut at 16 in Serie C1. His rapid progression — promotion through Italian divisions and a £2 million transfer to Sampdoria at 20 — was facilitated by Italy's deep football infrastructure and his natural ability. At Sampdoria, his partnership with Roberto Mancini ('The Goal Twins') and the backing of ambitious club president Paolo Mantovani created ideal conditions for his rise to European success by 25.
starting_point: Born to a self-made millionaire construction company owner in Cremona, Italy; raised in the Castello di Belgioso as the youngest of five children in a wealthy but disciplined household.
current_position: Died on 5 January 2023 at age 58 in London, England from pancreatic cancer; final role: former football player, manager, and member of Italy's Euro 2020 coaching staff under Roberto Mancini.

trajectory.event: Made his senior debut for Cremonese in Serie C1, the Italian third tier, playing alongside adults.
Signed by Sampdoria for £2 million after helping Cremonese achieve promotion to Serie A.
Won the Coppa Italia with Sampdoria, scoring in the final, and formed the 'Goal Twins' partnership with Roberto Mancini.
Won the European Cup Winners' Cup with Sampdoria, scoring both goals in the 2-0 final victory over Anderlecht.
Won Serie A with Sampdoria, the club's first-ever Italian league title.
Signed for Juventus for a then world-record fee of £12 million.
Won the UEFA Champions League with Juventus under manager Marcello Lippi.
Became player-manager of Chelsea after Ruud Gullit's sacking, winning the League Cup and Cup Winners' Cup.
Died on 5 January 2023 in London after a long battle with pancreatic cancer.
